analysis.one_liner: Expands border enforcement with thousands more agents, detention beds, surveillance technology, and a reorganized border agency.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late September 2006 with zero cosponsors, sent to five House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have dramatically expanded immigration and border enforcement: thousands of new Border Patrol and immigration enforcement agents each year, 25,000 additional detention beds per year, surveillance technology across every mile of the U.S.-Mexico border, radiation detectors at all ports of entry, and better pay and equipment for border agents. It would also have merged two major Homeland Security agencies into a single new bureau, reimbursed states that jail undocumented immigrants, and expanded cooperation with state and local police in immigration enforcement. It was referred to five committees and died without any of them taking action.
analysis.who_benefits: Border Patrol and customs personnel would get pay raises, student-loan repayment up to $80,000, body armor, night-vision gear, and better vehicles and radios. Border-state governments would be reimbursed for incarceration costs. Frequent cross-border travelers would get expanded, cheaper expedited-entry lanes. Homeland security contractors would gain from authorizations like $200 million per year for border surveillance systems, plus procurement of helicopters, boats, vehicles, and radiation portal monitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Border agents, border states, security contractors

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes at least 3,000 additional Border Patrol agents per year for fiscal 2007-2010, plus 2,000 immigration enforcement agents per year, and 400 more customs officers per year at ports of entry
Authorizes funding to add 25,000 immigration detention beds per year through fiscal 2010 to end what it calls 'catch and release'
Requires deployment of radiation portal monitors at all U.S. ports of entry to screen inbound cargo for nuclear and radiological material
Raises top Border Patrol pay from GS-11 to GS-12, allows up to $80,000 in student-loan repayment for agents, and extends law enforcement retirement coverage to inspection officers
Mandates body armor, night-vision devices, GPS units, encrypted radios, and police-type vehicles for every Border Patrol agent, with vehicles replaced every three years
Reimburses states for costs of incarcerating undocumented immigrants charged with crimes, and reimburses border property owners for damage caused by unlawful crossings
Requires a GAO study of deaths in immigration custody, including whether any personnel negligence or deliberate indifference was involved
Directs DHS to expand expedited-traveler lanes to all major ports of entry and lower their fees, letting vetted frequent travelers move through faster

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the bill's many open-ended authorizations, including $200 million per year for border surveillance deployment and 'such sums as may be necessary' for agents, detention beds, and equipment. Unauthorized immigrants would face far greater odds of detection, detention, and removal, and a new provision would make drunk driving a ground for deportation. Businesses relying on immigrant labor would face stepped-up employment-verification enforcement reports, and federal agencies would absorb a major reorganization.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes billions in spending with many 'such sums as may be necessary' provisions and no specified offsets, leaving the true cost to be filled in by later appropriations

It would merge Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement into a single new Bureau of Border Security and Customs, a restructuring whose disruption the bill never weighs against its claimed coordination benefits

It makes driving while intoxicated a basis for detention and deportation and encourages state and local police to enforce federal immigration law, expanding the reach of removal into routine local policing
It authorizes contracts with private companies to transport apprehended immigrants and directs full use of private detention space, channeling enforcement expansion through private vendors
The bill's central 'operational control' mandate requires preventing every unlawful entry across all land and maritime borders, a standard border experts have long treated as unattainable in full

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill paired genuinely useful elements — agent pay, body armor, port-of-entry screening, custody-death oversight, state reimbursements — with a very large, open-ended enforcement buildout whose costs it never quantified. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that billions in unspecified spending, a risky agency merger, and tougher treatment of immigrants with minor records were the price of the package, and Congress never got the chance to weigh them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2006 and referred to five House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Spratt Jr. of South Carolina introduced the bill in the House on September 29, 2006
No member signed on as a cosponsor

The bill was referred to the Homeland Security Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary, Government Reform, Armed Services, and Ways and Means committees, for a period to be determined by the Speaker
No committee took up the bill, and it never received a floor vote; the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no one gained its benefits and no one bore its costs: taxpayers were not billed for the new enforcement spending, unauthorized immigrants were not subjected to the expanded detention and removal machinery, and the proposed contractors got no new business. It simply added to the record of border-security proposals that never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained; costs never materialized

for.name: Rep. John M. Spratt Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured no cosponsors

against.name: House Homeland Security Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chair was a Republican in the 109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 29, 2006 and took no further action on the bill for the remainder of the Congress

against.name: House Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, Armed Services, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for provisions in their jurisdictions and never considered it

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; a single Democrat sponsored the bill and not even a cosponsor from either party signed on, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Border security and surveillance technology contractors
industries.note: The bill authorizes $200 million per year for full border surveillance deployment, plus radiation portal monitors, drones, sensors, and a Secure Border Initiative contract-review regime that assumes major industry contracts. Its interests run partly alongside public security goals but partly against taxpayers, since costs are open-ended.

industries.industry: Private immigration detention and transport companies
industries.note: The bill directs use of private space and facilities to expand detention capacity and authorizes private contracts to transport apprehended aliens, creating new revenue tied to detaining and moving more people. Its growth depends on enforcement against immigrants, whose interests run opposite.

industries.industry: Aerospace and vehicle manufacturers (helicopters, boats, patrol vehicles)
industries.note: Mandates at least 100 additional Border Patrol helicopters, 250 power boats, and a vehicle fleet with one police-type vehicle per three agents, all government procurement. Benefits flow to manufacturers but are funded by taxpayers.

States would be reimbursed for incarcerating undocumented immigrants charged with certain crimes, easing a cost states have long borne. Border property owners could also claim reimbursement for damage from unlawful crossings.

industries.industry: Federal border agencies (Border Patrol, customs and immigration enforcement)
industries.note: Personnel would get pay raises, loan repayment, equipment, and thousands of new positions, but the bill would also dissolve CBP and ICE into a single new Bureau of Border Security and Customs under a Senate-confirmed commissioner, forcing a major reorganization.
